belov.name: Andrey Belov
belov.role: Research fellow, scanning probe microscopy lab
belov.bio: Has worked with scanning tunnelling microscopes for twenty years: builds the instruments, teaches students to sharpen the tips, and argues about whether a picture of an atom can be called a photograph.
facts: Built his first microscope as a student, from parts of decommissioned equipment
Runs a nanophysics practical for third-year students
Believes a good experimentalist is half a plumber

lebedeva.name: Maria Lebedeva
lebedeva.bio: Works on numerical simulation of flows, from the air around a wing to mixing in chemical reactors. Writes popular science texts about why water is so complicated.
facts: Teaches a course on continuum mechanics

kotova.name: Irina Kotova
kotova.bio: Studies how the brain completes the picture of the world from incomplete data. Runs experiments with visual illusions and recordings of brain activity.

orlov.name: Dmitry Orlov
orlov.bio: Develops error-correction methods for superconducting qubits. Explains quantum computing without the words 'both 0 and 1 at once'.
facts: Leads a seminar for olympiad students

remizov.name: Pavel Remizov
remizov.bio: Studies who is responsible for the decisions of automated systems. Teaches technology ethics to future engineers.
facts: Author of the course 'Ethics for Engineers'
Believes philosophy should be taught together with programming

grishina.name: Elena Grishina
grishina.bio: Creates polymers that close cracks without human help. Will bring samples to the talk that you can cut and watch grow back together.

malinin.name: Sergey Malinin
malinin.bio: Builds numerical models of the atmosphere and the ocean and checks how well they predicted the past.
facts: Will explain how to read forecasts and their uncertainty

1.title: How to see an atom if it cannot be seen
1.announce: Light is too coarse a tool to see an atom. How physicists get around this limit with a needle, a current and quantum mechanics.
1.thought: To see an atom you do not have to illuminate it: it is enough to measure the current leaking through a gap one nanometre wide.

2.title: Why turbulence is still unsolved
2.announce: The equations of fluid motion were written almost two hundred years ago. Why a million dollars is still offered for proving a single property of these equations.
2.thought: We can write down the laws of water motion, but we cannot prove that these laws always have a sensible solution.

3.title: The brain that guesses
3.announce: Why we see things that are not there and miss what is in front of our eyes. Perception as a constant testing of guesses.
3.thought: The brain does not record the world: it keeps guessing it and corrects the guess by its errors.

4.title: What a quantum computer can do today
4.announce: Without the words 'both 0 and 1': what a qubit is, why it makes errors and when quantum computers will become useful.
4.thought: The main task of a quantum computer today is not to compute faster but to learn not to make mistakes.

5.title: Who is responsible for a machine's decision
5.announce: If an autopilot makes a mistake, is the driver to blame, the programmer, or nobody? A talk about where human responsibility ends.
5.thought: The more autonomous a system is, the harder it is to find the person responsible for its mistake, and this is not only a task for lawyers.

6.title: Materials that heal themselves
6.announce: Plastic that closes a scratch overnight and concrete whose cracks are sealed by bacteria. The speaker brings samples: you can cut them and watch them grow back together.

7.title: How climate is calculated
7.announce: What a climate model is made of, how it is tested against the past and how to read forecasts together with their uncertainty.
